Key conversion decisions:

- **Cast**: one box throughout — opens in B02, feeds B07's calendar, emits slices in B08. Zero pantry stills, zero segment cards, zero verdict card.
- **All body beats are Manim drawings**. Chart/search cards considered for B05–B06 and B02 but rejected by card-test question 3 in every case — the box cast draws the claim more directly.
- **7 source beats merged** (the five segment cards, V01 verdict, and BVDT) — their content is distributed across body beat narration and the BHTF discussion, not discarded.
- **BHTF prompt** is the original H01 health-check prompt, preserved verbatim and now read aloud per HANDOFF LAW, with two concrete viewer checks replacing the generic "apply what you learned" wording.

metadata.title: Claude, By the Numbers
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: show-tell style (Bear, 2026-09-26): opens on the hesitant writer + terms card, no verdict card; Your Turn is the Claude.ai composer; spoken outro stays.
metadata.audience: Solo operators and practitioners who have spreadsheet data they are afraid to look at
metadata.one_idea: Without the data plugin your numbers sit in spreadsheets you never open; with it Claude does data exploration and the unglamorous-but-essential data cleaning, then answers real questions (which clients are declining?) — but the analysis is only as trustworthy as the data and the assumptions, so you still own the judgment.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Somewhere on your drive is a spreadsheet you haven't opened in months. The question isn't whether you need SQL or formulas. You just ask Claude in plain English — and this film shows you how far that actually goes.
beats.motion_claim: The writer types the naive question (formulas required) and corrects it to the real one (plain English works) — the film's central claim, stated in the first beat.

beats.narration_text: Three terms. The data plugin: a Claude tool that reads and analyzes the spreadsheet files you point it at. An NL query: a plain-English question Claude converts into the right analysis. And revenue risk: when most of your income depends on just a few clients.

beats.narration_text: Start with the box you never open. Picture a year of revenue locked inside a folder labeled Finances, sitting on your drive, gathering dust. Not because it's empty. Because opening it means analysis, and analysis has always felt harder than it is.

beats.narration_text: Without the plugin, here is the pattern. Export a CSV. Open it. Stare at rows and columns until you get a vague sense of up or down. Close the file. Go back to work. The questions that actually matter go unanswered — not because they're hard, but because this loop never breaks.

shot.visual_intent: Four tiles arrange in a ring on the stage: 'Export CSV' → 'Stare at rows' → 'Vague sense' → 'Close file'; a terracotta arrow loops from the last tile back to the first.
shot.motion_claim: The loop closes on itself — nothing learned, nothing changed.

'Stare at rows' tile drops in at top-right
'Vague sense' tile drops in at bottom-right
'Close file' tile drops in at bottom-left

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell style: four tiles on cream stage; loop arrow is the new shape that lands after first frame.

beats.narration_text: With the plugin, you point Claude at that same box and ask the way you'd ask a colleague: which clients bring in the most revenue, and has the mix shifted? No formula. No pivot table. One question in, one sentence back.

shot.visual_intent: The same finances box from B00 — lid lifts; a question label enters from the left; a single sentence-tile floats out to the right and settles.
shot.motion_claim: One question in, one sentence back — the loop is broken.

beats.narration_text: Exploration first. Point Claude at a mystery file — cryptic column headers, dates in three formats — and it describes the structure, flags what's strange, and suggests the questions worth asking. Often the best question is not the one you started with.

beats.narration_text: Cleaning is the unglamorous prerequisite. Inconsistent dates, duplicate rows, impossible values — the plugin fixes them and reports exactly what it changed. That change log is not paperwork. It's the audit trail you verify before you trust the numbers built on top.

shot.visual_intent: Two data pages sit on the stage: the left one has red-marked cells (bad dates, duplicate rows); they correct one by one; on the right, a change-log strip accumulates a row per fix.
shot.motion_claim: Messy cells correct themselves; the log records every fix — the audit trail before you trust.

beats.narration_text: Visualization. Ask for a chart of monthly revenue and you get one — for a deck, for a partner, or just to feel your own trajectory. Line charts for trends. Bars for comparisons. Ask for something different and you get something different.

beats.narration_text: Comparison is where analysis earns its keep. Two periods, side by side — the delta between them is your trajectory. Totals tell you where you are. Comparisons tell you where you're heading. Building that by hand is tedious. Here it's one question.

shot.visual_intent: Two bar columns grow side by side on the stage, labeled 'Q3' and 'Q4'; a delta arrow draws from the top of Q3 to the top of Q4; an ink label 'trajectory' lands on the arrow.
shot.motion_claim: The gap between periods draws itself — trajectory made visible.

beats.narration_text: Make it a ritual. First of the month, ten minutes: point Claude at last month's revenue and expenses and ask for a health check. Total revenue, total expenses, margin, how it compares to the month before, anything that looks off. Do this every month and you're never surprised by your own numbers.

shot.visual_intent: An isometric calendar drops onto the stage; the '1' cell is circled in terracotta; the finances box slides in from the left; a second cycle shows the box sliding in again, then a third — a rhythm forming.
shot.motion_claim: The box shows up on the first, month after month — a ritual, not a one-time query.

beats.narration_text: Concentration risk is the most important thing a solo operator can know. If one client is forty percent of your income and you don't know it, you can't plan for the day they leave. Ask Claude: who carries most of my revenue, and is anyone quietly spending less?

shot.visual_intent: Revenue flows out of the box and splits into four client segments (page slices); one segment grows and crosses a terracotta risk ring; a terracotta dot marks the crossing point; label '40%' lands beside the oversized slice.
shot.motion_claim: One slice outgrows the others and crosses the risk line — concentration you can now see.

beats.narration_text: The honest part. The analysis is only as trustworthy as two things: the data you fed it, and the assumptions underneath it. The plugin tells you what it found and what it fixed. You verify the fixes before you trust the numbers built on top. You own the call.

shot.visual_intent: A balance beam sits on the stage; the left pan holds a stack of data pages labeled 'data quality'; the right pan holds a block labeled 'assumptions'; when both are solid the beam levels and an ink check mark rises above; one pan lightens and the beam tips — a terracotta warning dot appears.
shot.motion_claim: Trust swings with what you put in — the beam is the evidence; the call is yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I have a spreadsheet of my invoices and a spreadsheet of my expenses for the past year. First, tell me what's in each file and flag anything that looks messy or wrong. Then give me a business-health check — am I profitable month to month, which months were strongest and weakest, and is any expense category growing faster than revenue? Then tell me the one follow-up question I should ask next. Run it on your actual files. It turns this film into a five-minute conversation about your own money. Then check two things yourself: does every data fix in the change log look right to you? And does the follow-up question it hands back change what you would do next? Liam, in for Bear.

structured_output.notes:
**Object cast.** One hero object throughout: a cardboard box labeled "finances" (kraft faces, ink outlines per the isometric kit). Contents: data pages (rows of data, used in B03 as cryptic vs. described pages, and in B04 as marked vs. corrected cells). Processes: a loop ring of four tiles (B01), a question label + answer tile (B02), a change-log strip (B04), bar columns + delta arrow (B05/B06), a calendar page (B07), revenue slices (B08), a balance beam with two pans (B09). All objects share kraft/ink/cream from the isometric kit. Continuity: the finances box reappears in B02 (lid lifts), B07 (slides to the calendar), and B08 (revenue flows from it) — same box, whole film.

**Card choices.** Zero optional ShowTellCard beats in the body. A `chart` card was considered for B05 (visualization — bars grow, melt into a line) and B06 (comparison — two bars, delta), but both fail card-test question 3: the film's own cast (pages morphing into bars, bars with a delta arrow) shows the claim more directly and keeps object continuity per Law 4. A `search` card was considered for B02 (query → result) but fails question 3 for the same reason — the box opening shows the plugin's relationship to the file, not just the query pattern. The concentration-risk concept in B08 (one slice crossing a threshold ring) is a structural flow, not a number or interface, so it stays a drawing. All body beats use Manim.

**Open fact checks — carry into FACTCHECK.md before rendering:**
1. B03: Claim that the data plugin "describes structure, flags what's strange, and suggests questions worth asking" — verify against ch07-data.txt actual plugin feature documentation. UNVERIFIED from beat sheet alone.
2. B04: Claim that the plugin "reports exactly what it changed" (change-log feature) — verify this feature is present in the current data plugin as described in ch07-data.txt. UNVERIFIED.
3. B05: "Line charts for trends. Bars for comparisons" — verify these specific chart types are supported by the plugin; the source beat sheet mentioned them but the chapter is the authority. UNVERIFIED.
4. B08: "forty percent" used as a hypothetical threshold ("if one client is forty percent") — illustrative, not a published figure. EXEMPT (hypothetical framing preserved in narration).
5. B02/BDEFS: "three clients carry most of it" on the answer tile — also illustrative from the original one_idea field. EXEMPT.
6. BDEFS: "NL query" definition (plain-English → right analysis) — verify this matches the plugin's actual query mechanism vs. a SQL/Python backend. UNVERIFIED; may need qualifier.
7. General: The four capabilities (Explore, Clean, Visualize, Compare) sourced from B08 ChipGrid in the original — verify these are current and complete per ch07-data.txt. UNVERIFIED.

**Greeting check.** "Hallo" (German/Dutch) is listed in the skill's known-clean greeting list. Whisper-check the BIDEA beat after first Kokoro generation; re-voice from phonemes if it degrades.

**BIDEA correction logic.** Trigger "write your own formulas" appears verbatim in the text's third line. The corrected text reads: "The data plugin: / you point Claude at your spreadsheet / and then ask in plain English." — grammatically complete, the film's central claim. Misconception (formulas required) is the one the body dismantles through B02–B06. No punctuation ends the trigger or replacement.

**Estimated total duration.** Sum of estimated_duration_s: ~271 s (≈ 4.5 min). Timing is estimated at ~2.5 wps until narration is measured with Kokoro. Re-run generate_audio_kokoro.py, ffprobe each beat, write actuals back, and pad BOUT with its 1.0 s tail before the first art run.
